title: Multifamily Replacement Sourcing
name: Multifamily Replacement Sourcing
metaTitle: Multifamily Replacement Sourcing in Denver, CO
metaDescription: Sourcing apartment replacement properties for 1031 exchange investors across metro Denver, from RiNo new construction to Aurora and Lakewood value-add.

sections.html: Metro Denver's apartment market splits into two very different buyer pools right now, and an exchange investor needs to know which one they're stepping into before the 45-day clock starts. RiNo and LoDo are selling new construction at premium pricing with long lease-up runways. Aurora and Lakewood are selling older, cash-flowing buildings that need capital work. We source in both lanes depending on what the exchange budget and timeline can carry.

sections.heading: How the multifamily map splits
sections.html:
RiNo and LoDo have added a wave of new mid-rise and high-rise apartment product over the past several years, much of it built for renters moving into Denver from other Front Range towns and out-of-state relocations. That new stock trades at tighter cap rates because the buildings are new and the rent growth story is easy to tell a lender.

Aurora, Lakewood, and pockets of west Denver carry older garden-style complexes built in the 1970s through the 1990s. These trade at wider cap rates, carry real deferred maintenance, and reward a buyer who can handle unit turns and roof or boiler replacement without losing sleep. Both lanes qualify as like-kind replacement property; the difference is workload, not eligibility.

sections.heading: What the current demand story means for pricing
sections.html: Front Range in-migration keeps occupancy tight across most of the metro, which is good for an exchange buyer's income projections but bad for finding a discount. Sellers know demand is steady, so a buyer chasing a bargain in RiNo or LoDo is usually chasing the wrong submarket. Value-add plays in Aurora or Lakewood still carry more room to negotiate, especially on buildings that have sat with a tired unit mix or a landlord who stopped reinvesting years ago.

sections.heading: Where the 45-day clock gets tight
sections.html: New-construction lease-up buildings in RiNo move fast once they list, sometimes under contract within a week of hitting the market, which leaves little room for an investor still deciding on financing. Older value-add buildings in Aurora and Lakewood tend to sit longer, giving more breathing room to run numbers before locking in an identification. We usually recommend having at least one property from each lane on the identification list so a fast-moving deal in one submarket doesn't force a rushed decision in the other.

sections.heading: Building types in the pipeline
sections.html:
Across both lanes, the properties we track most often fall into a short set of categories:

  • New mid-rise apartment buildings in RiNo and LoDo with completed lease-up
  • Garden-style value-add complexes in Aurora and Lakewood
  • Small infill multifamily buildings of eight to thirty units near transit corridors
  • Townhome-style rental communities in the southern suburbs
  • Mixed-income complexes with a portion of units under a Denver affordability agreement

sections.heading: Watchouts before we put a building on the list
sections.html:
A mixed-income building with affordability-restricted units needs its compliance documents reviewed early, since those restrictions affect achievable rent and can slow a lender's underwriting. Older Aurora and Lakewood buildings need a real look at galvanized or polybutylene plumbing, since a full re-pipe can eat a year of cash flow if it's missed during diligence. We flag both before a building goes on the final identification list, not after.

Unit mix matters too. A garden-style complex in Lakewood built heavy on one-bedroom units competes for a narrower renter pool than one with a real spread of studios, one-bedrooms, and two-bedrooms, and that spread affects how quickly the building re-leases after a resident moves out. We ask for the current unit mix and turnover rate on every candidate rather than relying on the seller's average occupancy figure alone, since a building can show 95 percent occupancy overall while one unit type sits vacant for months at a time.

We also ask how a seller handles pet policy and short-term guest fees, since these smaller income lines add up across a hundred-plus unit building and a seller who's left money on the table there often has room elsewhere too.

faqs.q: Should I target new construction in RiNo or an older value-add building in Aurora for my exchange?
faqs.a: It depends on your timeline and appetite for capital work. New construction gives steadier income with less landlord work but a tighter cap rate. Value-add buildings in Aurora or Lakewood cost less per unit but need a buyer ready to fund unit turns and deferred maintenance.

faqs.q: Does a mixed-income building with affordability-restricted units still qualify as 1031 replacement property?
faqs.a: Yes, the restriction is a use covenant, not a property type issue, so it doesn't affect like-kind status. It does affect achievable rent and financing, so we flag it early for review.

faqs.q: How quickly do RiNo and LoDo apartment listings move once they hit the market?
faqs.a: New lease-up buildings in those submarkets can go under contract within a week of listing. If a property in that pool is on your identification list, financing should already be lined up before you sign.

faqs.q: What's the biggest cost surprise on older Aurora or Lakewood apartment buildings?
faqs.a: Plumbing. A lot of garden-style buildings from that era used galvanized or polybutylene pipe, and a full re-pipe can run well into six figures depending on unit count. We check for it before recommending a building for identification.

faqs.q: Can I put both a new-construction and a value-add building on my identification list?
faqs.a: Yes, and we usually recommend it. New-construction buildings in RiNo move fast, so having a slower-moving value-add option in Aurora or Lakewood as a backup keeps you from feeling rushed into a decision.
